stories.title: The political power struggles behind Taiwan’s referendum on nuclear power
stories.summary: Taiwan will hold a fourth referendum on nuclear power alongside local elections amid shifting public opinion on energy policy. Opposition parties use referendums on issues like nuclear power and crime to mobilise conservative voters and gain advantage in local elections. Critics warn frequent referendums risk becoming partisan tools rather than direct democracy, causing voter fatigue and reducing meaningful public debate on complex issues. Taiwan will hold yet another referendum on nuclear energy policy alongside local elections in November, prompting questions on the role of direct polls in the island’s domestic politics. As hustings for the Nov 28 “nine-in-one” elections heat up, referendums are one of the levers political parties are pulling to sway the island’s voters. Experts say that these political considerations hold equal, if not greater, significance for the politicians involved. The upcoming referendum on nuclear power will be the fourth on Taiwan’s nuclear policy in eight years, with the last one held just a year ago. It asks whether “the government should abolish its ‘Nuclear-Free Homeland’ policy to protect public health, ensure stable and affordable electricity supplies, strengthen national defence resilience and support the development of artificial intelligence industries”? Three proposed referendums were submitted to the Central Election Commission (CEC) this year, and only this one was approved. The CEC rejected a proposal for a referendum to legalise caning for serious crime, stressing that it would go against human rights. The other referendum rejected was on using all revenue from traffic fines to improve road safety and subsidise public transport. The CEC said that both the caning and traffic fine questions did not fall within the scope of matters that can be put to a referendum under Article 2 of the Referendum Act.

stories.title: US seriously considers use of nuclear weapons in Europe — Russian MFA
stories.summary: MOSCOW, August 29. US military strategists are seriously considering the possibility of using nuclear weapons in Europe, Russian Foreign Ministry special envoy. Andrey Belousov said in an interview with RT. According to the diplomat, Washington’s efforts to initiate discussions on Russia’s non-strategic nuclear weapons serve to divert international attention from what he described as the threat posed by US nuclear weapons stationed in Europe, as well as Washington’s nuclear missile programs and plans. "Speaking of this danger, it is impossible not to note that Washington’s insistence on initiating discussions at various multilateral disarmament forums on Russian non-strategic nuclear weapons, which do not threaten US territory, suggests that American military strategists are seriously considering the possibility of using nuclear weapons in the European theater of military operations," he said. "Obtaining objective data on Russian non-strategic nuclear weapons through negotiations or discussions on strategic stability, the introduction of intrusive transparency measures, or their reduction - and especially their complete elimination - would increase the likelihood of a scenario involving the use of nuclear weapons by the US and its allies in Europe," Belousov added. The diplomat stressed that European countries should recognize the full danger of what he described as Washington’s purely practical approach to the territory of its allies.

stories.title: French poll predicts Le Pen's victory in 2027 presidential election runoff
stories.summary: PARIS, August 29. Marine Le Pen, the National Rally’s presidential candidate, could win France’s 2027 presidential runoff regardless of her opponent, according to a poll conducted by Elabe for BFMTV and La Tribune Dimanche. Among 1,500 French adults surveyed online from August 26-28, 52.5% said they would vote for Le Pen in the second round if she faced former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe, the candidate of the centrist Horizons party. Philippe is considered the most likely contender to advance to the runoff against the National Rally candidate and is seen as having the strongest chance of defeating her. Le Pen’s projected margin is wider against other potential opponents. She could win 57% of the vote against former Prime Minister Gabriel Attal, the Renaissance candidate, or against Raphael Glucksmann, leader of the center-left Place Publique party. In a runoff against Jean-Luc Melenchon, the candidate of the left-wing France Unbowed party, Le Pen could secure 69.5% of the vote, according to the poll. Le Pen also leads in the first round. The pollsters examined six scenarios involving different combinations of candidates and political forces. In all six, Le Pen comes first, with between 34% and 35.5% of the vote. Melenchon ranks third in three scenarios, with 14-14.5%, while placing second in the other three. Philippe comes second in every scenario in which he runs, with between 17% and 20.5%.

stories.title: The rise of Thai beauty: The push to become South-east Asia’s beauty powerhouse
stories.summary: Thai beauty products are gaining popularity for their quality, local ingredients and suitability for Southeast Asian skin and climate – an advantage brands are pitching as they expand beyond Thailand. T-Beauty brands use social media and cultural influence to expand regionally and rival established K-Beauty and Western brands, with Ingu Skin’s strong Singapore debut and Mistine’s success in China showing that their appeal can travel beyond Thailand. Thailand’s growing cosmetics industry sees strong export potential, but faces stiff competition from J- and K-Beauty and increasingly competitive Chinese brands, even as rising demand could benefit local agriculture and the wider economy. Thai actress and model Chanana Nutakom is used to putting on copious amounts of make-up for work. After four decades in the business and countless Thai drama series, the 62-year-old celebrity knows better than most the importance of taking care of her skin – and is increasingly mindful of what she puts on her face. Chanana, better known as Dee, doesn’t just rely on pricey foreign skincare products to maintain her youthful appearance. She also uses Thai beauty products, or T-Beauty. “Expensive doesn’t always mean better and affordable doesn’t mean bad. What matters is the quality,” she told. The Straits Times. T-Beauty brands – ranging from fast-growing labels like INGU Skin to established household names like Srichand – are increasingly looking beyond their home market. They are betting that products developed with the South-east Asian climate and skin types in mind will give them an edge as they take on established Japanese and South Korean beauty brands and increasingly competitive Chinese rivals.
